newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - Rhone-Poulenc Rorer sees higher 97.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Rhone-Poulenc Rorer sees higher 97.

text.p: Rhone-Poulenc Rorer Inc, the pharmaceuticals unit of Rhone-Poulenc SA, said on Monday it expected net earnings for 1997 to be 15 to 20 percent higher than the $3.16 per share it earned in 1996, and it expected total sales to be eight to nine percent higher.

In an interview with Reuters, Rhone-Poulenc Rorer Chief Financial Officer Patrick Langlois said, "For total RPR in 1997, we believe earnings should increase in the range of 15 to 20 percent, compared to 1996 and in 1998, earnings should accelerate as well."
Rhone-Poulenc Rorer President Tim Rothwell said the company expected total sales growth of between eight and nine percent in 1997 versus 1996.

In 1996, Rhone-Poulenc Rorer's net attributable income rose 25 percent to $428.7 million, while its earnings per share were up at $3.16. The company said earnings would have been higher but for the costs of an albumin product recall at the Centeon LCC joint venture with Hoechst AG of Germany.
Sales were $5.420 billion from $5.316 billion in 1996 with a 36 percent rise in sales of Lovenox/Clexane anti-thrombosis drug to over $400 million.
Langlois said the company's 1997 earnings growth estimate included any possible future earnings adjustments due to Centeon.
"There will be some impact from Centeon but any possible adjustments have been taken into account in that 1997 estimate," Langlois said.

Centeon restarted its production on January 24 after an October 10 product recall for a potential risk of bacterial infection. Rhone-Poulenc Rorer said the 1996 costs of the recall were $0.44 per share.
Langlois said the company would not ship the albumin product in the first quarter 1997, due to the lag time between production and shipments.
"There are also a lot of uncertainties regarding the product and its market share position," he said.

As for other products, Rothwell said in 1997, the company expected to double worldwide sales of its cancer drug Taxotere, which was launched in the United States and Europe in the second quarter of 1996. In 1996, Taxotere had sales of about $90 million, it said.
Most analysts had expected Taxotere sales to be between $70 million and $75 million in 1996, Rothwell said.
Rothwell also said the company expected continued sales growth for Lovenox/Clexane, used to prevent deep-vein thrombosis.
"We have a number of clinical trials ongoing which we believe will result in continued growth and we expect to see sales of $500 million for this product as we go forward," Rothwell said.

CFO Langlois also said he expected the company to divest some assets in 1997 but that divestitures would be less significant than they were in 1996. In 1996, Rhone-Poulenc Rorer said it divested over $850 million in assets.
"There could be some (asset sales) in 1997, and going forward our strategy will be to focus on our key therapeutic areas," he said.
Results in 1996 were also helped by about $150 million in synergies derived from integrating the Fisons acquisition into Rhone-Poulenc Rorer, the company said.
Langlois and Rothwell said the company expected to generate a further $200 million from such synergies in 1997.
"The integration is proceeding on schedule," Rothwell said. "In 1997, we should benefit from the full-year impact of synergies."
As for the company's expansion in Asia, the company said it had established a regional branch in Hong Kong and was embarking on plans to increase its presence in China.
Rhone-Poulenc Rorer shares were trading off 2 at 74 at 1110 EST/1610 GMT.
